distillate: Plan: keep two scenario-generation models side by side — the existing hand-built discrete scenario set (a handful of named, hand-weighted regimes) and a new stochastic Monte Carlo world that samples scenarios from parametric distributions. Both implement the same weighted-scenario array type, so the evaluator, tuner and research-generation pipeline consume either unchanged; a single environment variable selects which world a run uses (default = discrete, "mc" = Monte Carlo), and the two are never mixed inside one run. Per-scenario UI visualization stays on the legible named discrete world regardless of which world drives the leaderboard. Alternatives considered: (a) replace the hand-built discrete world outright with the Monte Carlo world, which is a drop-in substitute that fixes the discrete set's overfit-to-hand-picked-points weakness; (b) keep only the hand-built world and hand-author more regimes to cover the gaps; (c) blend draws from both worlds within a single evaluation run; (d) drive the dashboard visualization off the dense samples as well.
authored: You decided to let both worlds coexist rather than pick one. The hand-built discrete world is legible — named regimes with explicit probabilities, which is what makes the dashboard readable and what lets a human argue with the prior — but it is a frozen snapshot of hand-picked points, so tuning can overfit to those points and the set goes stale. The Monte Carlo world fixes exactly that: sampled draws, equal weight per draw, honest tails without hand-authoring. You did not want to throw away either property, so you made them interchangeable behind one type: if both are just a weighted-scenario array, the evaluator, tuner and generator never need to know which one they got, and there is no duplicated evaluation logic. Selection is a single environment variable because that is the cheapest possible switch and it makes the choice a per-run property rather than a code change. You made the worlds strictly non-mixing inside a run so that no result is ever a silent average of two different priors. And you kept the UI on the named discrete world in all cases, because a few hundred anonymous draws make no sense in a dashboard.
resolution: Shipped as designed and held for roughly three weeks, with two later consequences the record ties back to it. Immediately it worked: an out-of-distribution validation pass was built directly on the coexistence property — strategies tuned on the discrete world re-scored against a dense sampled world without re-tuning — which promptly caught real overfit. Consequence one, ~11 days later: because every research script set the switch to the sampled world and the validation flag was coded as "not-sampled and not explicitly disabled", production output carried no validation metadata, and the leaderboard's upside and downside-floor columns were silently hidden in the deployed UI. The fix was to run production generation in discrete mode instead, which restored the columns. Consequence two, about three weeks later: the hand-authored discrete world was replaced as the default scoring prior by a distribution-reduced projection of the sampled world, explicitly so that the dashboard world and the leaderboard world would be projections of one distribution and "can no longer drift apart"; the legacy hand-built world was demoted to an opt-in third mode. The switch mechanism itself, the shared scenario type, and the never-mix rule were never reverted.
core_problem: The single global per-run world switch with strictly non-mixing worlds meant the mode production actually ran in silently suppressed the out-of-distribution validation output, hiding leaderboard columns in the deployed UI; and the two independently maintained priors stayed free to diverge until the hand-authored world had to be replaced by a reduction of the sampled world so they could not drift apart.

distillate: Plan: remove perfect-timing credit from the deterministic evaluator. Entries into the hedging leg currently assume execution at the exact cycle peak; exits and repurchases assume execution at the exact low. Introduce an entry haircut constant so the hedge ladders in roughly 10% below the peak, and route both the exit and the repurchase through one shared pricing helper that clears at the low times a repurchase haircut — a helper until now used only by one of the three paths. The solvency check continues to stress-test at peak notional for conservative capital-requirement estimates. Alternatives considered: (a) leave the exact peak/bottom execution assumptions in place, on the grounds that the inflation applies uniformly to every strategy and so does not distort comparisons; (b) apply the haircut arithmetic separately at each call site instead of consolidating behind one shared helper.
authored: You decided to strip the perfect-timing premium out of the evaluator because it was crediting executions no one can actually hit: entering at the precise top and exiting, plus repurchasing, at the precise bottom. That inflates expected terminal value and, worse, it rewards exactly the strategies whose edge depends most on timing, which is the opposite of what you want a ranking to do. So you laddered the entry to open about 10% below the peak via a new haircut constant, and you made both the exit and the repurchase clear above the low. You put that behind a single shared pricing helper rather than repeating the multiplication at each site, because one of the three paths already had this haircut and the other two did not — one helper means the three cannot drift apart the next time you retune the constant. This is deliberately symmetric with the earlier fix that introduced realistic pricing for the held position: the evaluator should be pessimistic about execution everywhere, not just in the one place you happened to look first. You left the solvency stress test anchored at peak notional, because there the conservative direction is to assume the largest exposure.
resolution: Shipped and held. The immediate measured effect was exactly the intended one: expected terminal values dropped across all strategies as the timing premium came out, while the relative ordering was unchanged and the top-ranked strategy retained rank #1 — the pre-fix ranking had been built on inflated but uniformly inflated numbers. The record afterwards shows the two constants being generalized rather than questioned: about a week later, during a multi-asset refactor, the shared pricing helper and the haircut were imported into the step-rendering module and into the structure-tree module, including a bugfix that added the haircut multiplier to a per-asset pricing path. An architecture review days later describes the haircut mechanics as settled parts of the model. Searching the record forward through mid-July turns up no reversal, no re-tuning of either haircut value, and no regression attributed to the change.

distillate: Plan: move caching off local files and into a remote database, covering two use cases — a position-level cache and a cache of grid-search / parameter-tuning results — so that expensive multi-minute grid searches are shared across machines, worktrees and runs instead of recomputed. Alternatives considered: (a) an edge-deployed hosted SQLite service with replication; (b) a serverless autoscaling Postgres service. The two are weighed on latency, cost, scalability and operational complexity of the caching layer.
authored: You decided the tune cache had to live in a remote database rather than on local disk. A single grid search costs minutes and can run to hundreds of thousands of evaluations, and you are running the same searches from multiple worktrees and machines; with a local cache file every worktree starts cold and recomputes work another one already did. Both things you want to cache are simple key/value blobs looked up by a content hash, not relational data you will ever join or query analytically, so the access pattern does not argue for Postgres. That pushes you toward the hosted SQLite option: it keeps the schema trivial, keeps the client dependency light, and edge replication keeps read latency low, which matters because the whole cache is bulk-loaded once per process. Serverless Postgres would give you more engine than the workload needs and more operational surface for the same benefit. The remaining question is whether the cheaper option's write path stays consistent when several worktrees tune in parallel, which is what an upsert on conflict has to handle.
resolution: The SQLite-compatible option was chosen and Postgres was not adopted; the record shows no later migration or reversal. The backend was consolidated within about a day: the full test suite passed after integration, and the design was documented as a key/name/value table with a write-through upsert specifically so parallel worktrees stay consistent, with a graceful fallback to a local file when no database URL is configured. It worked in practice — a production generation run reused 28/28 grid-search results with zero re-tunes — and it continued to serve as the persistence layer through subsequent refactors. Two follow-up incidents were configuration, not engine, problems: the credentials file was resolved only from the current working directory, so worktrees silently fell back to local storage and re-tuned from cold (fixed by a walk-up env loader), and the same symptom recurred later because the env file was not loaded into the dev runtime at all. No observation through mid-July reverses the choice, migrates to Postgres, or attributes a regression to the engine itself.

distillate: Plan: add a tunable slippage parameter (0–1) to the leveraged-hedge backtest so that a forced close fills not at the exact trigger price but at trigger ± (fraction × the bar's overshoot beyond the trigger), thread it through backtest → optimizer → CLI environment variable, and run a sensitivity comparison at 0 / 0.5 / 1.0 to measure how much unmodeled tail risk the optimizer has been ignoring. The current model assumes forced closes always fill exactly at the trigger price, which is the most optimistic assumption for high leverage; the historical bars available report only period high/low, not the true intra-period fill. Alternatives considered: (a) keep the existing exact-trigger fill model and rely on the existing leverage-penalty regularizer as the sole tail-risk control; (b) hard-code a single pessimistic assumption instead of exposing a tunable fraction; (c) default the parameter to 0 so legacy behavior is preserved unless explicitly opted into.
authored: You decided to model gap-through fills on forced closes because the existing backtest assumed the position always closes at exactly the theoretical trigger price, and that is the best case — it systematically flatters high-leverage hedges and makes you unable to tell whether an unhedged position genuinely matches hedged performance across volatility spikes. Once a close triggers intra-period, price often keeps running, so the realized fill can be worse than the trigger; on a thin-margin high-leverage position that means realized loss can exceed the nominal margin. You made it a fraction from 0 to 1 rather than a fixed pessimistic constant so you could run a sensitivity sweep instead of just swapping one arbitrary assumption for another, and you defaulted it to 0 so nothing about existing results changes unless someone opts in. You threaded it end to end — backtest option, optimizer interface, and a CLI environment variable — so the whole sweep could be run from the command line without code edits, and the plan was to compare the resulting leaderboards to see whether the high-leverage candidates lose their appeal once realistic slippage is priced in.
resolution: The feature was implemented end to end and then fully reverted within roughly one hour of the same session. The plumbing worked: typecheck was clean and three optimizer runs at fraction 0, 0.5 and 1.0 all completed without error. But the three runs produced bit-for-bit identical leaderboards — same top-5, same winner at the same return, same leverage distribution across the top-20 — so the parameter had zero effect on strategy selection under any assumption. A targeted probe on an aggressive high-leverage spec over a 180-day window found the cause: zero forced-close events ever triggered in the historical data, because period-close bars never violated the trigger boundary. The conclusion recorded was that the bar granularity available is too coarse to surface the intra-period tail events where gap slippage matters, making the model dead code. The gap-fill logic was removed from the backtest and then the parameter was stripped from the optimizer interface and the CLI, returning all three files to their pre-implementation state. The pre-existing leverage-penalty regularizer was left as the tail-risk control.
core_problem: The model's premise was wrong for the data on hand — the available bar granularity never produces a forced-close event at all, so the entire slippage refinement was unreachable code and was reverted in full.

distillate: Plan: feed an out-of-distribution robustness signal to the generating model through its prompt context rather than into the objective it is tuned against. Each candidate the search loop scores on the small hand-built discrete scenario set is additionally re-scored, without re-tuning, on a densely sampled world (256 samples), and the outcome is rendered inline on the leaderboard the generator already reads — either a robustness score, or an overfit tag counting how many sampled worlds breach the hard feasibility constraint. The same tag is persisted into the explored list and the cross-run ledger so the signal survives across runs, and a short prompt block teaches the generator to prefer structures that survive the sampled continuum over ones that only win the named scenarios. Gated by a flag that disables it. Alternatives considered: (a) run the sampled world inside the tuning hot loop, i.e. re-tune every candidate against it — the most faithful signal but the expensive one, since cost lives in grid search, not evaluation; (b) apply it post-hoc as a filter or re-ranking after the search finishes, leaving the search itself unguided.
authored: You decided to put the robustness signal at the prompt level, not in the tuning loop and not as a post-hoc filter. The reason is a cost asymmetry you had already established: the sampled world is expensive because of tuning (grid search multiplied by scenario count), not because of evaluation — re-scoring an already-fixed plan on N sampled scenarios is linear and effectively free. So you can afford to compute it once per scored candidate at 256 samples and still not touch the hot loop. The problem you are solving is that the generator was learning to exploit the gaps in the small discrete world: it would find configurations that win the named scenarios but breach the feasibility cap across the sampled continuum. Filtering those out afterwards wastes the iteration — the generator never learns why. Instead you show it the verdict where it already looks: the leaderboard line gets a robustness score when the structure holds up, or an overfit tag with the failure count when it does not. You also carry the tag into the explored list and the cross-run ledger, so a dead end stays diagnosed across sessions rather than being re-proposed. Net effect: the signal steers the search cheaply instead of policing it expensively.
resolution: The feature shipped and remained in service. It was opened as a PR the same evening with typecheck clean and 49/49 tests passing, and merged shortly after with a clean 66/66 suite. It was used in production runs immediately: the next morning's automated run initialized with robustness checking enabled at 256 samples against a 25-structure ledger. By three days later the mechanism was load-bearing in the loop's architecture — the causal-tagging function emitted the overfit tag as one of a prioritized set of dead-end reasons fed back to the generator, and the ledger showed the signal firing as designed, with 8 of 11 recorded attempts flagged as overfitting the named scenarios. The record shows no reversal and no regression traced to this decision. Two later touches are adjacent but are not corrections of its premise: the call site was updated during a project-wide objective-function migration that touched every scorer call site alike, and a robustness badge column was dropped from the dashboard as part of a table-simplification change — the read-only reporting surface, not the feedback path, which the later edit confirms was still live.

distillate: Plan: treat the hand-played round of the search loop as validation of the harness and move the next phase to model-generated hypotheses. Three candidates were hand-written into a generated directory and scored through the shared evaluation harness; a diversified variant scored highest, ahead of the single-item variant and the baseline, and the complexity penalty plus structural dedup demoted the more baroque combinations as intended. The run also exposed two model weaknesses: a flat global depth constant that makes the optimizer indifferent to which item is chosen, and evidence that the diversified form beats the single-item form. Next phase replaces the hand-written definitions with model-generated ones running through the same evaluation and ranking pipeline. Alternatives considered: (a) stop here, package the hand-played variant, and defer automation; (b) fix the exposed model weaknesses first, so the automated phase optimizes against an honest model, rather than automating on the current model and correcting later.
authored: You decided the hand-played round had done its job and that the next phase should be model-generated hypotheses. Your reasoning: the point of playing the loop by hand was never the three candidates themselves, it was to prove out the surrounding machinery — file-based generation, a single unified evaluation harness, and fitness-based ranking with a complexity penalty and structural dedup. All of that held. The diversified variant beating both the single-item variant and the baseline by a wide margin told you the fitness signal has real dynamic range, and the simplicity judge correctly demoted the baroque combinations, so the penalty and dedup mechanisms are working as designed rather than just being present. That is exactly the precondition for automating: if the scoring harness could not separate good from bloated, pointing a generator at it would just produce noise faster. You also came out of the round with two concrete model gaps rather than vague unease — the flat depth constant makes the choice arbitrary, so the optimizer is picking on numerical noise instead of economics. You chose to close the model gap before automating, so that when the generated phase runs, the answers come from real signal rather than a model artifact the generator could learn to exploit.
resolution: Both parts of the plan were carried out and held. The model gap was closed within minutes of the decision: the flat depth constant was replaced with per-item depths and a carry-cost model was added. Re-running the evaluation on the corrected model confirmed the hand-played conclusions were not artifacts — absolute returns fell across the board due to the newly priced carry cost, but the ranking was preserved and the diversified variant remained top, still 63% ahead of the baseline. The automation phase was then built the same day: a headless harness that spawns a generator to propose one candidate per iteration, scored by the same deterministic tuner against the same leaderboard, at roughly $0.1 per iteration. That harness became the project's primary search mechanism for the following two weeks, accumulating a cross-run ledger, dedup by structure signature, and causal dead-end tagging, and it produced winners promoted back into committed code. The window through late June shows no reversal of the automation decision and no regression traced to it.

distillate: Plan: extend per-item concentration measurement in the scorer from the terminal snapshot to the whole cycle. Exposure will be computed per phase as well as at the terminal state, weighted by a per-item risk table, aggregated, and subtracted from the fitness score as a new additive penalty term. The measured exposure and its dominating moment will also be surfaced as a tag in the generating model's prompt and as a badge on the dashboard. Landing it bumps the tuning cache version and requires re-freezing the golden fixture and re-tuning. Alternatives considered: (a) keep the existing terminal-only per-item weight cap, which already limits any single thin item's share of the final state; (b) define per-phase exposure as held value only, versus held value plus recycled positions plus borrowed notional plus unsold remainder; (c) penalize absolute exposure versus net signed exposure; (d) aggregate phases by worst-case path-max versus time-weighted average versus keeping the single terminal snapshot; (e) reuse the existing cap thresholds versus introducing separate thresholds for the in-cycle measure.
authored: You decided to measure per-item concentration risk across the entire cycle rather than only at the terminal state, because the cap you shipped previously only sees the end state. A strategy can take on a large notional of a thin, illiquid item at the peak and carry that exposure all the way down through the decline, and if the item is not in the final holdings your existing cap never sees it — yet the portfolio genuinely bore that risk. So you are computing exposure per phase, weighting each item by how badly it behaves in a drawdown, taking the worst moment across the cycle plus the terminal state, and subtracting a coefficient times that expected exposure from fitness as its own penalty term. You are making it a smooth, continuous penalty rather than a hard constraint so that a strategy can still take the exposure when the returns clearly justify it. You are putting the computation in the composition module so there is a single source of truth. You are also feeding the resulting tag into the generator prompt so candidates are steered away from risky carries in the first place. You accept that this bumps the cache version, moves the golden set, and forces a re-freeze and a re-tune.
resolution: Shipped the same day in two commits (core penalty plus dashboard visualization) and opened as a PR. Exposure was implemented as path-max across phases plus the terminal state, weighted by the per-item risk table, with the penalty subtracted from fitness; the risk table and coefficient were added to the cache key, the cache version was bumped, and the golden fixture was re-frozen. Verification passed 44/44 tests and the leaderboard was unchanged at the top. The term held as one of five independent additive penalties in the fitness function through the following two weeks. Then the objective was replaced wholesale: a risk-averse certainty-equivalent score became the sole objective, and the arithmetic formula was deleted. In that refactor the cycle-exposure penalty — together with the downside, tail-risk and terminal concentration penalties — was explicitly demoted to "DIAGNOSTIC ONLY — retained for the UI/leaderboard, no longer folded into the score." The stated reason was that the risk-averse utility already prices those downside cases. The terminal concentration haircut survived inside the new score; the cycle-exposure penalty did not. The next day the dashboard was corrected to stop showing cycle-risk as a fitness deduction. The exposure metric and its badge survived as reporting; the penalty mechanism stopped affecting ranking about ten days after it shipped.
core_problem: The dedicated additive cycle-exposure penalty stopped influencing ranking ten days after shipping, when a risk-averse certainty-equivalent objective replaced the additive penalty stack on the explicit grounds that the utility already prices the same downside — leaving the cycle-exposure work as a display-only diagnostic.

distillate: Plan: remove eval from the parallel parameter-grid tuner. Currently the tuner serializes the scoring function once per run via toString() and each worker thread reconstructs it with eval before scanning its slice of the grid. Instead, add an optional source-metadata field {module, name} to the item interface, populate it at the collection boundaries, ship that metadata in the grid-job payload in place of the function string, and have each worker dynamically import the module and look the item up by export name, with a per-worker cache keyed by module#name. Items that carry no source metadata (inline test fixtures, ad-hoc constructed objects) are guarded out of worker dispatch entirely and fall through to the existing single-threaded inline scan. Alternatives considered: (a) keep the toString-plus-eval path as it stands; (b) instead of falling back to single-threaded execution for items without source metadata, route them through the existing dynamic-import helper already used by the runtime loader.
authored: You decided to stop shipping the scoring function to workers as a string and eval-ing it there, and to have workers import the real module instead. The eval path works, but it is the kind of thing you want out of the codebase: the function arrives as text, gets rebuilt at runtime, and you have already had to patch it once to cope with helper wrappers the bundler injects into the serialized source. Since every item that matters is defined at a known collection boundary, you can simply record where it came from. So you are adding an optional source tag to the type, threading it through the dispatch function and the job payload in place of the function string, and having the worker await a dynamic import and pick the named export out of the module. You are caching the import per worker so the cost is paid once. You are making the source field optional deliberately so the change is backward compatible: anything constructed inline, such as a test fixture, simply has no source, so you guard the dispatch on its presence and let those fall through to the inline scan rather than adding a second code path. Nothing about the grid math changes.
resolution: The refactor landed as a squash commit. Within the same day the parallel tuning path was found to be broken. In the project's TypeScript-loader-plus-worker-threads setup, a worker thread cannot resolve the .js-suffixed import specifiers that the TypeScript sources emit, so importing the generated index threw on one of its child modules. The worker error set the pool-broken flag, and because that flag gates all future dispatch, every tuning run silently fell back to single-threaded execution. The refactor's own verification had passed only because the single-threaded fallback produces identical results, so the loss of parallelism was invisible to it. A first fix was attempted — registering the TypeScript loader inside the worker pool — but it did not resolve runtime specifier mapping, since the problem was module resolution rather than transpilation. The change was then reverted whole, opened as a PR with the regression analysis and merged to main, with the full suite green at 91/91. The recorded rationale for reverting rather than continuing to patch was that the serialize-plus-eval approach never imports modules inside workers and is therefore immune to the resolution problem, and that parallelism outweighed the cleanliness gain of dropping eval.
core_problem: Import-based worker dispatch could not resolve the emitted .js module specifiers under the TypeScript loader inside worker threads, so every tuning run degraded silently to single-threaded via the pool-broken fallback — undetectable by the change's own verification because the fallback returns identical results — and the refactor was reverted in full within a day.

distillate: Plan: replace the flat $8-per-rebalance transaction-cost assumption in the trace CLI with a context-aware default — $8 on the primary network (and on the fallback path where no network id is present), $0.50 on the four supported secondary networks — while keeping the existing environment-variable override as the first check. The context-aware value is passed into the optimizer both in the main trace flow and in the width-comparison path, and the dashboard panel switches to a small-value currency formatter so sub-dollar costs render correctly. The premise is that repositioning is a fixed per-transaction cost set by the network's fee market, not a function of position size. Alternatives considered: (a) leave the flat $8 default in place and require callers to set the existing environment-variable override for every secondary-network run; (b) model the reposition cost as scaling with position size or deployed capital rather than as a fixed per-transaction charge.
authored: You decided to make the reposition cost depend on the network instead of hardcoding one number. The position the dashboard actually analyses is on a secondary network, but the analysis was charging it the primary-network figure — which over six repositions in the backtest window came to $48 against a real cost nearer $3. That silently over-penalized rebalancing economics and made the whole strategy look worse than it is. You reasoned it through from what the operation actually costs: repositioning is a fixed per-transaction cost the fee market sets, with no dependence on how much capital sits in the position. So you put a small context-aware default in the trace CLI that checks the environment override first, then falls back to the high figure only for the primary network and the unknown-network case. You threaded the resulting value into both places the optimizer is called, including the width comparison, so every variant is scored under the same cost assumption. And you switched the UI to a small-value formatter, because the existing one would not show a fifty-cent figure honestly. You expect this to move the reported numbers but not the ranking — it is an accuracy fix on the economics, not a strategy change.
resolution: Shipped as planned. Implementation, typecheck, and the unit suite (23/23) all passed with no regressions; the change was committed on a branch and opened as a PR. The regenerated trace confirmed the intended effect: the persisted cost parameter dropped to 0.5, total reposition expense fell from $48 to $3 across the same six repositions, final value and total return rose accordingly, and strategy selection was explicitly unchanged. The dashboard was deployed the same day and the live trace was fetched and verified to serve the corrected values. The record shows no reversal, no correction of the fixed-per-transaction premise, and no regression traced to this change through the latest related observations three weeks later, which concern unrelated work. One scoping fact from the record, noted without any observation treating it as a defect: the context-aware default was implemented in the trace CLI, and later records still document a flat default for the same parameter in the backtest/optimizer layer and its presets.

distillate: Plan: extend the search loop's candidate registry so each entry stores not only its structural identity (a hash of its source) but also the free-text hypothesis the generating model stated for why the candidate should work. The hypothesis is preserved across re-scores, surfaced trimmed to 140 characters in the explored-candidates list fed back to the generator, and added to the persistent registry schema. Alternatives considered: (a) keep the registry keyed on structural identity alone, since structurally identical candidates already collapse to one entry and dedup works as intended; (b) additionally store and replay the stated hypothesis.
authored: You decided the registry should remember not just what was tried but why. Structural dedup already collapses syntactically identical candidates to one entry, so the generator does not literally repeat itself — but it can re-dress the same idea in a different structure and get a fresh entry, which means it explores the same hypothesis several times while believing it is covering new ground. Storing the stated rationale fixes that at the level where the waste actually happens: the explored list the generator reads back now carries a short note of the idea behind each dead end, not just its shape. You preserve the rationale on re-score with a null-coalescing fallback, because a candidate re-scored under a new objective or a new world is the same idea and should not lose its provenance. You put the field on both the in-memory entry type and the persistent schema so it survives across runs, and you trim it in the display so the feedback block stays cheap in prompt tokens.
resolution: Shipped the same day. Typecheck passed on both packages and all 6 registry unit tests passed, covering unified identity, registry recording, infeasible handling, board layout, robustness scoring and the explored-list display with the new field threaded through. The change was committed alongside a prompt sharpening in the same session. The registry continued to be developed on top of the field rather than around it: within hours a dual-backend registry with objective-tag scoping was documented, and a unified board assembly deduping in-code candidates against the enumerated registry top was added. The record through mid-July shows no reversal, no removal of the field, and no regression traced to it.

distillate: Plan: add an optional size-multiplier knob to the hedge parameter set so the computed hedge size can be scaled above 1 (over-hedging: more downside protection at the cost of upside drag) or below 1 (under-hedging: more upside captured, more downside exposure), defaulting to 1 so existing behaviour is preserved, and apply the multiplier at both hedge-sizing paths in the backtest loop so a parametric sweep can search for the best size. Alternatives considered: (a) leave hedge size fully determined by the existing capital-efficiency sizing formula, which already derives a size from the position summary; (b) expose it as a tunable knob with a neutral default.
authored: You decided to make hedge size a tunable knob rather than a derived constant. The sizing formula gives one answer — the capital-efficient size — but that answer encodes a particular point on the downside-protection versus upside-drag trade-off, and you have no evidence it is the right point. Rather than argue about it, you exposed it as a multiplier so the optimizer can sweep it and the data can answer. You defaulted it to 1 so nothing about existing results moves unless someone opts in, which keeps the change backward compatible and keeps prior runs comparable. You applied it at both sizing sites — at initialization and at the trigger path where the hedge opens on a downward breach — because a multiplier that only reached one of them would silently mean different things for different strategy shapes.
resolution: Applied to both sizing paths the same day, with both defaulting to 1.0 when unspecified. The backtesting harness became operational with ranked results the same afternoon, and the knob entered service as one dimension of the parameter sweeps: later records describe sweeps over multiple hedge and width combinations, and further knobs were added alongside it rather than replacing it. The optimizer subsequently grew a hedge-kind parameter, per-width robust optimization, and margin-cost pricing in the fitness function, all built on the same parameter set. The record through mid-July shows no reversal, no removal of the multiplier, and no regression traced to it.

distillate: Plan: replace the band-width comparison sweep, which tunes a single timing parameter per width while holding every other knob fixed and ranks results by final value on one historical path, with a full robust optimization: for each band width, generate up to 700 candidate parameter sets tuning every knob, evaluate each across many overlapping historical sub-windows (default 90-day windows at 15-day steps), and select the configuration maximizing mean return minus standard deviation across those windows. Non-primary rows let the hedge type vary freely per width; the deployed strategy is preserved as a primary row for direct comparison; the table ranking switches from final value to the robust score; the UI is rebuilt around robust statistics with an explanatory note; window size, step and sample budget become environment variables. Alternatives considered: (a) keep the single-path per-width sweep ranked by final value; (b) full per-width robust optimization across overlapping windows.
authored: You decided the width comparison had to be optimized robustly rather than on a single path. Ranking by final value over one historical trajectory selects whatever happened to fit that trajectory — it is single-path overfitting wearing a leaderboard, and it gets worse the more knobs you let it touch. So you moved to mean minus standard deviation across many overlapping sub-windows: a configuration only wins if it does well on average and does not fall apart in particular regimes. You also stopped pinning every other knob while sweeping one, because a per-width answer that holds the rest fixed is not really the best strategy for that width, it is the best timing parameter given someone else's choices. You let the hedge type vary freely on non-primary rows for the same reason. You kept the deployed strategy as a primary row so the comparison stays honest, rebuilt the table around robust statistics so the number people read is the one being optimized, and added a note explaining the methodology, since a ranking by a score nobody understands is worse than no ranking. Window sizing and sample budget go to environment variables so the cost can be matched to the machine and the dataset.
